title: De quibusdam eximiis proprietatibus circa divisores potestatum occurrentibus

deep.reconstruction:
Page 266–267 continues the series of 'particular theorems' that Euler derives from the residue tables of §38. Throughout the memoir, q=2p+1 is an odd prime not dividing a. Then a^{2p}−1 = (a^p−1)(a^p+1) ≡ 0 (mod q), so q divides exactly one of the two factors. Earlier in the paper Euler shows that q | a^p−1 exactly when a is a quadratic residue mod q; this is Euler's criterion, a^{(q−1)/2} ≡ (a/q). His empirical claim is that this choice depends only on the residue class of q modulo 4a, and is the same for q ≡ r and q ≡ −r. That is Euler's formulation of quadratic reciprocity together with its supplements.

The page gives the tables for four values of a, each indexed by q mod 4a:
- Theorem 9 (§40), a=12, classes 48n±r: r=1, 11, 13, 23 give 12^p−1; r=5, 7, 17, 19 give 12^p+1. Equivalently (3/q)=1 iff q≡±1 (mod 12).
- Theorem 10 (§41), a=13, classes 52n±r: r=1, 3, 9, 17, 23, 25 give −1; r=5, 7, 11, 15, 19, 21 give +1. Equivalently (q/13), since 13≡1 (mod 4).
- a=14, classes 56n±r: r=1, 5, 9, 11, 13, 25 give −1; r=3, 15, 17, 19, 23, 27 give +1. The classes ±7 and ±21 are rightly omitted because 7 divides them.
- a=15, classes 60n±r: r=1, 7, 11, 17 give −1; r=13, 19, 23, 29 give +1.

The page is followed by the Additamentum, which begins Euler's attempt to prove such statements.
errors: No mathematical errors. I checked all entries with modern reciprocity: for a=12, (3/q); for a=13, (q/13); for a=14, (2/q)(7/q) with (7/q)=(−1)^{(q−1)/2}(q/7); for a=15, (3/q)(q/5). Every row agrees.

Minor redundancy rather than an error: for a=12 the modulus 48 is larger than needed, since the dependence is only on q mod 12. Euler keeps 4a uniformly. Some listed classes, e.g. 52n±25 at n=0 or 56n±9, are not primes themselves; the classes are still correct for the primes they contain.
No proof is given; the tables are read off the residue lists. Euler admits the gap on the next page ('firmis demonstrationibus destituuntur').

ideas.what: q=2p+1 prime divides a^p−1 or a^p+1 according as a is or is not a quadratic residue mod q
ideas.where_published: E262 (Theoremata circa residua ex divisione potestatum relicta) and this memoir E557

ideas.what: The quadratic character of fixed a at prime q depends only on q mod 4a and is symmetric under q→−q; tabulated for a=12–15
ideas.usually_credited_to: Conjectured by Euler (E164, 1744; E552, E557); first proved by Gauss (1796, Disquisitiones 1801), with partial work by Legendre (1785)
ideas.where_published: E164; E552; E557 (Opuscula analytica I, 1783); discussed in Weil, 'Number Theory: An Approach through History', and Lemmermeyer, 'Reciprocity Laws'

deep.surprise_reason: The page consists of correct tables illustrating Euler's well-documented empirical form of quadratic reciprocity in a famous memoir. Nothing here is absent from the historical literature.
transcription_corrections: The transcription matches the image. In the scan the a=15 row for r=13 is printed with a defective numeral ('ic. n + 13'); it should read 60.n ± 13 | 15^p + 1, as transcribed.
On page 266, 'a = 13.' at the bottom is a catchword for the table on page 267, not a separate heading.
Page 266 prints 'sive forma 12^p − 1 sive 12^p + 1' (minus first), and §41 similarly prints 'a^p + 1, sive a^p − 1'. The order in the transcription is immaterial.
